find: A <dfn class="term" data-def="Digital Audio Workstation — software used to record, edit and produce music on a computer.">DAW</dfn> is a software application for recording, editing and producing music. But the software is only part of the picture — it relies on a range of hardware components to function.
replace: A <dfn class="term" data-def="Digital Audio Workstation — the hardware and the software together that make up a computer-based music production system.">DAW</dfn> means the hardware and the software together: the computer and the devices plugged into it, plus the program that records and edits the sound.
note: F1: spec defines a DAW as both the hardware and the software elements, not software alone

expect: Digital Audio Workstation — software used to record, edit and produce music on a computer.
value: Digital Audio Workstation — the hardware and the software together that make up a computer-based music production system.
note: F1: glossary matched the software-only definition

expect:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of multiple specifications with clear links to production workflow.
Mid band (3-4): Sound analysis of at least two specifications.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of one spec.
Indicative content: RAM — more RAM means more tracks, plug-ins and virtual instruments running simultaneously without crashes; CPU — faster processor handles real-time effects and instrument processing; SSD — faster load times for samples and projects, reduces latency; Display — larger/higher-res screen improves workflow with complex mixer views; OS — determines DAW compatibility. Credit discussion of bottlenecks, upgradeability, budget considerations.

find: For plug-in questions, know the difference between EQ (frequency), dynamics (volume) and modulation (time-based) effects.
replace: For plug-in questions, know the difference between EQ (frequency), dynamics (level), time-based effects (reverb and delay) and modulation effects (chorus, flanging and phasing).
note: F4: the spec lists reverb and delay as the time-based effects; modulation is a separate category

expect:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis covering multiple plug-in types with clear explanation of their sonic impact.
Mid band (3-4): Sound analysis of at least two plug-in types.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification.
Indicative content: EQ shapes the tonal balance (boost/cut frequencies, remove muddiness, add clarity); dynamics processing (compressor controls dynamic range for consistency, limiter prevents clipping, gate removes unwanted noise); reverb/delay add spatial depth and ambience; modulation adds movement and texture; distortion adds character and energy. Credit examples of specific use cases and how plug-ins work together in a mix chain.

expect:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion covering multiple editing tools with clear explanation of how each addresses the stated problems.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good coverage of several tools with some application to the scenario.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant tools identified.
Lower band (1-2): Limited identification.
Indicative content: Timing — quantise to snap notes to grid, with swing or humanisation to maintain natural feel; manual note editing on piano roll to move/delete specific notes. Volume — edit velocity values for individual notes; apply compression plug-in to even out dynamic range; use automation to control volume changes over time. Additional refinement: adjust note lengths, correct wrong pitches on the grid, add pitch bend or modulation data. Export settings for final output.

expect: What is the advantage of a 'workstation' DAW over a cloud DAW?
value: What is the advantage of a desktop DAW over a cloud-based DAW?
note: F5: the spec names the two types as cloud-based and desktop; the answer already says desktop

find: Displays — staring at computer screens for extended periods causes eye strain, headaches and fatigue.
replace: Displays and workstations — staring at computer screens for extended periods causes eye strain, headaches and fatigue. Poor posture at a badly set up desk or chair causes back pain.
note: F6: spec hazard is 'use of computer displays and workstations'; back pain is its risk

find: can cause falls, resulting in back pain, sprains or fractures.
replace: can cause falls, resulting in sprains, breaks or bruising.
note: F6: the spec pairs slips, trips and falls with sprains and breaks

find: Four studio hazards and their risks: noise (hearing loss), displays (eye strain), slip/trip/fall (back pain, sprains), electrical (electrocution).
replace: Four studio hazards and their risks: noise (hearing loss), displays and workstations (eye strain, back pain), slip/trip/fall (sprains and breaks), electrical (electrocution).
note: F6: key fact repeated the wrong hazard-to-risk pairing

find: Displays — position screens at eye level, adjust brightness, take regular screen breaks
replace: Displays and workstations — position screens at eye level, set the chair so your back is supported, adjust brightness, take regular screen breaks
note: F6: control measure must cover the posture risk as well as the eyes

expect:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of all three settings with clear explanation of their impact.
Mid band (3-4): Sound analysis of at least two settings.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification.
Indicative content: Bit depth — 24-bit captures wider dynamic range than 16-bit, reducing quantisation noise; if set too low, recordings lose detail. Sample rate — higher rates (48/96 kHz) capture more frequency detail but create larger files; must match the target format. Buffer size — small for recording (low latency) so performers hear themselves in real time; large for mixing (stable processing with more plug-ins). Incorrect settings can cause poor quality recordings, latency issues during performance, or system instability.

expect:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion covering all four hazard types with appropriate control measures and a systematic approach to risk assessment.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good coverage of multiple hazards with relevant control measures.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some hazards identified with basic measures.
Lower band (1-2): Limited response.
Indicative content: Conduct a risk assessment before use. Noise — set maximum volume levels on monitors and headphones, limit session lengths, provide breaks. Displays — position screens correctly, adjust brightness, enforce screen breaks. Cables/equipment — use cable management to prevent trips, keep walkways clear, store equipment when not in use. Electrical — PAT test all equipment, check cables for damage, avoid overloading sockets, use RCDs. Reporting — establish a system for reporting hazards and incidents. Student induction/training on safe use of equipment.
